entities.name: Epicydes
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Epicydes, a Greco-Carthaginian of Syracusan lineage, emerged as a pivotal military and political figure during the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE), initially serving as an emissary and officer in Hannibal Barca's army before becoming a co-leader of the Syracusan resistance against Roman expansion. His career is intrinsically linked to the dramatic final years of independent Syracuse, a city whose strategic importance in the central Mediterranean made it a critical prize for both Rome and Carthage.

Dispatched to Sicily in 214 BCE alongside his brother Hippocrates, Epicydes skillfully exploited a burgeoning anti-Roman sentiment within Syracuse following the death of its long-standing ally, Hiero II. After the assassination of the pro-Roman regents, Epicydes and Hippocrates successfully rallied the Syracusan populace, seized control of the city, and formally allied with Carthage. For two years, from 213 to 211 BCE, Epicydes spearheaded the desperate defense of Syracuse against the relentless siege led by the Roman general Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a conflict famed for the innovative defensive machines designed by Archimedes.

Epicydes's tenacious leadership, though ultimately unsuccessful, prolonged the siege and exacted a heavy toll on Roman forces, demonstrating the formidable challenge posed by Carthaginian-backed resistance. His fall with Syracuse in 211 BCE marked the definitive end of the city's independence and cemented Rome's complete dominance over Sicily, transforming the island into a crucial Roman province. The brutal sack of Syracuse, a direct consequence of its defiance under Epicydes, served as a stark warning to other potential rebel cities.

The determined resistance led by Epicydes and Hippocrates transformed the Siege of Syracuse into one of the most memorable and protracted engagements of the Second Punic War, etching their names into the annals of military history as the last champions of an independent Hellenistic Sicily.
